analysis.one_liner: Phases oil and gas drilling on Colorado's Roan Plateau while protecting its wildlife habitat and waterways.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee in April 2008 and died there when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set the terms for natural gas drilling on federal land atop Colorado's Roan Plateau. It would designate Special Protection Areas where no drilling equipment could touch the surface, allow leasing only one development tract at a time, ban oil shale development, cap total surface disturbance at 350 acres, and require companies bidding for leases to pay minimum bonus amounts to boost federal and state revenue. It was a compromise: it would permit drilling to go forward, but slowly and with strict environmental conditions instead of the faster plan the Bureau of Land Management had approved.
analysis.who_benefits: Hunters, anglers, and outdoor recreationists who use the Roan Plateau, along with nearby communities concerned about water quality in the Parachute Creek and Northwater Creek drainages. Federal and Colorado treasuries would also gain, because the bill would require competitive bonus bids and phased leasing designed to bring in more revenue than rapid leasing would [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill would designate Special Protection Areas covering critical wildlife habitat and the watersheds of Northwater Creek and the East Fork of Parachute Creek, managed to prevent irreparable damage to fish and wildlife, and it would attach nonwaivable no-surface-occupancy conditions to any lease touching those areas [S2] [S3].

It would limit drilling to one phased development tract at a time, and the next tract could be leased only after 90% of recoverable gas was produced and 99% of disturbed land reclaimed in the previous tract, reducing habitat fragmentation and duplicative roads and pipelines [S3].

It would bar oil shale exploration and development in the planning area entirely, cap unreclaimed surface disturbance at 350 acres, and let the Secretary demand bonus bids and lease sizes above standard limits to maximize returns to the United States and Colorado [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies would bear slower, more costly development: phased leasing, mandatory unitization agreements covering all leases in a tract, reclamation standards, and nonwaivable surface protections. Energy production from the plateau would come online more slowly than under the Bureau of Land Management's 2007 plan [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill would still authorize industrial drilling on top of the Roan Plateau, a habitat the bill itself describes as home to genetically pure Colorado River cutthroat trout, mule deer, and Rocky Mountain elk; conservationists who wanted full protection would see the bill as legitimizing development on a fragile landscape [S3].

Phased development would slow gas production: no second tract could be leased until wells in the first recovered at least 90% of its gas, which delays energy output and the associated royalty stream during a period of high natural gas prices [S3].

Requiring every lessee to join a federal unitization agreement, while reducing redundant infrastructure, could concentrate development decisions in a single unit operator selected under the agreement [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This was a genuine compromise rather than a one-sided bill. The public would keep access to protected watersheds and habitat, recover more federal and state revenue through higher bonus bids, and avoid the patchwork of scattered drilling pads, while industry would still get access but on a slower, stricter schedule. The real objection cuts both ways: it gives up full protection of the plateau's top, and it gives up speed of development. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how much one values intact trout habitat and hunting grounds versus faster gas production.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Natural Resources Committee and two of its subcommittees in April 2008, and it sat there without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. John Salazar of Colorado introduced the bill on April 17, 2008, joined by Rep. Mark Udall of Colorado as its one cosponsor [S1] [S3] [S4].

The House referred it to the Committee on Natural Resources the same day, and a week later to two subcommittees, the Subcommittee on National Parks, Forests and Public Lands and the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources [S1] [S5].
No further action was taken, and the bill died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies were able to obtain leases on the Roan Plateau in 2008 under the Bureau of Land Management's faster plan, without the bill's phased-development requirements and nonwaivable surface protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas companies that leased in 2008

for.name: Rep. John Salazar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to impose phased development and surface protections on Roan Plateau leasing.

for.name: Rep. Mark Udall
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as its only cosponsor.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chairman Nick Rahall, D-WV)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 17, 2008, and never scheduled a markup or floor action before the Congress ended.

against.name: Bureau of Land Management
against.role: Interior Department land management agency (Bush administration)
against.what_they_did: Proceeded in 2008 with leasing the Roan Plateau under its 2007 record of decision, so drilling went forward without the bill's phased-development conditions.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Colorado Democrats sponsored the bill and no vote was ever taken, so no partisan pattern shows up in the record.

industries.note: The bill would let companies lease and drill on the Roan Plateau, but only one tract at a time, with mandatory unitization, higher bonus bids, and nonwaivable no-surface-occupancy rules in sensitive drainages. The industry favored faster development under the Bureau of Land Management's plan, so its interest in the bill ran against the conservation and revenue protections ordinary taxpayers and outdoor users would have gained.
The bill would prohibit any oil shale exploration or development in the planning area, closing off a speculative extraction opportunity in a fragile watershed.
